name: Esther Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Esther, thanks for doing this. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to tech firms, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office for a small architecture practice, nine people above a bakery near the station. I do the diaries, the planning application paperwork, invoicing, supplier orders and the files for every project. I use AI tools every day: I've got one that reads supplier invoices and drafts them into the accounts, and another that turns the partners' voice notes into meeting minutes. I like building little systems that make the place run smoother.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay is low for what I do, and I've got about three weeks of money saved because rent here ate everything when I moved out of my parents'. I share a flat with my friend Ruth. There aren't many offices in this town, so if this job went I'd be looking at a long commute or a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, the tools are still useful, just not magic. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use. Online I'd probably post something nerdy about my invoice setup and get three likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's safe in that world, but I'm still underpaid and three weeks from broke. The tools save me five hours a week, and the firm just fills those hours with more work, not more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for a raise in January, with a list of what my systems save them in hours. I'd keep tinkering with the tools. And I'd start doing small setup jobs for other local offices on Saturdays, because I'm not going to get rich waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. A bit impatient, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools barely improve, what happens to the systems you've built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They keep working. They're boring but solid. If nothing radical changes, the person who knows how to make the boring tools useful is worth a bit more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pay is low. Does AI Plateau change how you'd push on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a better case, if anything. I can show I'm doing the work of one and a half people. Whether they pay for it is another thing, because small firms always say money's tight.

I'd post about my **invoice setup** to anyone who'll listen.

Saved hours get filled with **more work**, not more money.

Do small **Saturday setup jobs** for other local offices.
Keep improving the **invoice and minutes** tools.

fieldNote: She's **comfortable with the tech** and sees herself as the office's toolsmith.
Her pressure is **pay and savings**, not job security.
She turns frustration into a **side hustle** rather than waiting.

steps.text: Bring a list of hours saved to the January pay talk
Set up invoice tools for other local offices on Saturdays
Keep improving the voice-note minutes tool for the partners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make work better, but only if the people doing the work share in what's saved. I'd be pushing for a four-day week at the practice rather than one fewer job. Online I'd be sharing what I've learned so other admins don't get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm both the person who could build the new system and the person it replaces. The partners like me, but they also like a lower wage bill. I think I'm fine for a few years if I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retitle myself, basically: go to the partners and propose a practice operations role, running all the software and the planning portal work. I'd do an online course in workflow automation in the evenings. And I'd grow the Saturday work into a proper side business with a website, maybe fifty pounds a job to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exciting, mostly, with a knot underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your systems are part of the change. Does that make you safer or less safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Every system I build makes the office need less admin, so I'm either running the systems or I've trained my replacement. If they buy something off the shelf instead, it's the second one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if office jobs in town shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the tools. I'd blame the people who decide the savings go to the owners and not the staff. And a government that hasn't touched employment rules in years.

fieldNote: She sees the **double edge** of her own work clearly, without being paralysed by it.

Thin savings mean her plan relies on **keeping this job** while she grows the side business.

steps.text: Pitch a practice operations role to the partners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to fight for a share of the gains, loudly. I'd be in every group chat telling people to sign up for whatever campaign is pushing for a basic income. At work I'd be honest with the partners that we need a plan for everyone, not just them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my office job and my side business both go at once. The thing I'm selling is setting up tools that will soon set themselves up. Everything I do is thinking work. I'm adaptable, but two years doesn't leave much to adapt into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze as much as I could out of the next two years: say yes to every setup job, take my income up and bank all of it. I'd look hard at work that's partly hands-on, like site coordination for builders, since robots come later. And I'd be out campaigning for income support, because I don't think any one person outruns this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit wired. Like running for a train I might not make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028, robots around 2031. How does that play out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partners would probably need fewer of us too, since drawings and planning applications are thinking work. Building sites would still need people for another three years. So I'd try to get onto a site with one of our contractors, coordinating deliveries and safety paperwork, where someone has to be there in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruth think? Would the flat survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's a primary school teaching assistant, so she'd probably keep working longer than me. We'd keep the flat if one of us was earning. If we both lost work, I'd honestly have to go back to my parents' spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, if we get organised. At work I'd raise a staff plan for the practice. Online I'd keep sharing what's changing so people can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got about three good years of the side business and the operations role, then it gets very thin. The question is where I am when that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to build the side business up to a few regular clients, and save half of what it brings in. I'd do a short course in construction site management, because that's the bridge into hands-on work. And I'd talk to the partners about helping me get on a site team in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit scared. But I feel like I'd be ahead of most people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build or learn in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Site management, mainly. I'd keep learning the AI tools too, because the person who uses them best on a site is useful longer. But I wouldn't bet my rent on staying a tool person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave town for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. There are more building jobs in the city. Ruth would hate it, but I'm twenty-seven with no kids, so if anyone can move for work, it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to bring everyone along, and that's what I'd push for. At work I'd suggest the practice train the drafters and admins together. Online I'd probably start a little newsletter for office admins on what's changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly opportunity, if I don't get lazy. I'd have time to build a real business and a real skill, and still have room to change again before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the practice job for a few years and make the operations role real. I'd grow the side business properly, with an accountant and a website. And from the start I'd save a fixed amount each month, because I've never had a cushion and I'd like one before anything big lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. Uneasy, but in a way that makes me move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Would you keep the architecture job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For three or four years, yes. It's steady and I like the people. After that I'd want to be running my own thing or managing sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently because you know where it ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not get comfortable. Ten years sounds like forever, and I know myself, so I'd set a date every year to check what I'm doing. Like a check-up at the dentist.

I'd start a **newsletter** for office admins about what's changing.
think: For me it's mostly **opportunity**, if I don't get lazy.
I have time to build **a real business** and change again before robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm good with these tools and even I can't see a way through in two years. What would help is income support that kicks in fast, and help to move into hands-on work while there's still time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether admins get any credit. We're the people making these tools work in real offices, and we're paid the least. I'd like someone to notice that before they replace us.

headlineQuote: We're the people making these tools work in real offices, and we're paid the least.
portrait: Esther runs a **small architecture office** and uses AI tools every day.
She's underpaid with **three weeks of savings**, so she builds a Saturday side business.
She sees herself as **both builder and target** of office automation.
Fast AGI pushes her towards **site work** and campaigning; ten years feels like opportunity.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even her tool skills don't buy her a way through in two years.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast income support** and help moving into hands-on work while there's time.
